text.en: Meena saw the periodic table on the lab wall. "Elements in the same column behave alike," said her teacher.

The Modern Periodic Law says that the physical and chemical properties of elements are periodic functions of their atomic numbers. The table has seven periods, which are horizontal rows, and eighteen groups, which are vertical columns, and elements in a main-group column often have similar outer-shell electron arrangements and similar properties.
Periodic trends are patterns across a period and down a group. Atomic radius generally decreases across a period and increases down a group. Ionisation enthalpy, the energy to remove an electron, generally rises across a period and falls down a group, and electronegativity follows a similar pattern.
Most metals lie to the left and centre, most non-metals to the right, and several metalloids between them. Hydrogen is a non-metal in the top-left corner. The chapter also connects metal properties to ores, extraction, alloys and corrosion. Understanding periodic trends helps us predict reactions and uses of elements.
The Modern Periodic Law says that the physical and chemical properties of elements are periodic functions of their atomic numbers.
The modern table has seven periods and eighteen groups. Elements in a main-group column often have similar outer-shell electron arrangements and similar properties.
Periodic trends are patterns across a period and down a group.
Atomic radius generally decreases from left to right across a period and increases down a group.
Ionisation enthalpy, the energy to remove an electron, generally rises across a period and falls down a group, and electronegativity follows a similar pattern.
Most metals lie to the left and centre, most non-metals lie to the right, and several metalloids lie between them. Hydrogen is a non-metal in the top-left corner.
Understanding periodic trends helps us predict reactions and uses of elements.
Each element has a definite number of protons. Sodium has eleven and magnesium has twelve, so sodium comes first.
Atoms of one element can have different neutron numbers, but they have the same proton count. They occupy the same position in a table ordered by atomic number.
Read left to right for increasing atomic number within a period. Move down a column to compare members of a group.

board.text: Periods are rows and groups are columns

text.en: Sodium and magnesium have electrons in three shells. They are in period three, but magnesium has one more outer electron, so it lies in the next group.
Lithium, sodium and potassium are group one metals. Their similar outer-shell arrangement helps explain why they often form ions with a charge of plus one.

board.text: Li, Na and K all have one outer electron

text.en: Chlorine has seven outer electrons and commonly forms a chloride ion by gaining one. Argon already has a full outer shell under the school model.

board.text: Halogens and noble gases have different outer shells

text.en: Helium is a noble gas even though it has only two electrons. The first shell is full at two.

board.text: Helium fills its first shell with two electrons

text.en: Across the main groups of one period, added protons tend to pull outer electrons closer while those electrons enter the same main shell.

board.text: Across a period, the nucleus attracts outer electrons more strongly

text.en: Potassium has an additional occupied shell compared with sodium. Its outer electron is farther from the nucleus and partly screened by inner electrons.

board.text: Down a group, additional shells increase size

text.en: First ionisation energy measures the energy needed to remove the first electron from an isolated gaseous atom. It shows general trends, with exceptions.
An atom with greater electronegativity draws shared electrons towards itself more strongly. This is a different idea from removing an electron from a separate atom.

board.text: Electronegativity describes attraction in a bond

text.en: Sodium is generally larger than magnesium in the same period. Potassium is larger than sodium in the same group.
Silicon lies near the boundary used to distinguish many metals from non-metals. Its behaviour can be useful in semiconductor materials.
A mineral is a naturally occurring substance. A material is called an ore when it can supply a valuable metal economically.

board.text: A mineral and an ore differ

text.en: An ore may occur with rock and other unwanted material. Concentration separates part of the unwanted material before extracting the metal.
A very reactive metal holds on to its compounds strongly. Industrial extraction may need electrical energy. Less reactive metals can often be obtained by other methods.

board.text: Extraction decisions depend on the metal

text.en: Bauxite is an important source of aluminium. Haematite is a source of iron, and copper pyrites is one source of copper.

board.text: Aluminium, iron and copper have different ores

text.en: After extraction, the metal may still contain impurities. Refining is the later stage used to improve the metal’s purity.
An alloy combines a metal with other elements. Brass combines copper and zinc. Stainless steel contains iron and chromium, which helps it resist corrosion.
Iron can corrode when moisture and oxygen are present. Rust weakens an exposed iron surface over time.

board.text: Rust requires iron, water and oxygen

text.en: Paint helps keep water and oxygen away from iron. Galvanising coats iron or steel with zinc to protect it.
Salt and moisture can accelerate corrosion. The textbook’s Pamban Bridge case shows why engineering choices and protective maintenance matter.

board.text: Coastal bridges face humid, salty air

text.en: Use atomic number and electron arrangement to explain a position or trend. Use the metal’s properties to reason about its uses, alloys and protection.

board.text: Use the chapter in two ways

problem.en: Does atomic radius increase or decrease across a period?

text.en: Across a period the nuclear charge increases.
Electrons are pulled in closer.
So atomic radius decreases.

problem.en: An atom has arrangement 2, 8, 2. Locate its period and main group.

text.en: Three shells contain electrons, so it is in period 3.

why.en: Count the occupied shells in this main-group example.

text.en: Two outer electrons identify it with group 2. Its atomic number is 12, so it is magnesium.

why.en: Add all shell counts to find the number of protons in a neutral atom.

problem.en: Which is generally larger, Na or Mg? Which is larger, Na or K?

text.en: Na is generally larger than Mg.

why.en: They are in period 3. The larger nuclear charge in Mg tends to pull its outer electrons closer.

text.en: K is larger than Na.

why.en: K has an additional occupied shell.

problem.en: Why coat steel used near the sea?

text.en: Moisture and salts make corrosion a greater concern.

why.en: Corrosion depends on the environment around the metal.

text.en: A suitable intact coating limits contact with the environment.

why.en: The coating protects the underlying steel from rapid attack.

prompt.en: A friend says Elements in a period have similar properties. How will you reply?

requiredIdeas.en: Elements in a group have similar properties.
They have the same outer electrons.

points.en: Atomic radius generally falls across a period.
First ionisation energy generally rises across a period.
Elements in a main-group column often have similar outer-shell arrangements.
